pr_title: Add support for multi-segment parameters to gRPC JSON transcoding
pr_body:
Fixes https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/34524

gRPC JSON transcoding supports parameters that span multiple segments. This isn't in ASP.NET Core routing and errors if given this syntax.

For example: `/v1/{book=shelves/*/books/*}` specifies as mult-segment `book` parameter. It matches `/v1/shelves/james/books/cool-book` and the parameter has the value `shelves/james/books/cool-book`.

New in this PR is a parser that understands this routing syntax and adapts it to ASP.NET Core route.

_From @JamesNK on Tuesday, July 20, 2021 2:15:48 AM_

Hi

This feature could be difficult. The non-wildcard routes maps directly to the existing ASP.NET Core route syntax. However, wildcard routes will need to be rewritten inside the library before they can be used. That might be simple, or it could be quite difficult.

I don't have much time to work on GrpcHttpApi for the rest of this year, I have .NET 6 features to deliver, but if someone wants to attempt it then a PR is welcome.

We've moved this issue to the Backlog milestone. This means that it is not going to be worked on for the coming release. We will reassess the backlog following the current release and consider this item at that time. To learn more about our issue management process and to have better expectation regarding different types of issues you can read our [Triage Process](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/master/docs/TriageProcess.md).

I ran into this issue recently when using:

```xml
<PackageReference Include="Microsoft.AspNetCore.Grpc.JsonTranscoding" Version="7.0.0-preview.4.22251.1" />
```
and version 7.0.100-preview.4.22252.9 of the .Net SDK.

This was pretty surprising to me since the [documentation for http.proto](https://cloud.google.com/service-infrastructure/docs/service-management/reference/rpc/google.api#google.api.HttpRule) specifically shows examples of using "*" as wild card to match against any path segment.  

The lack of this capability seems like it will also impact API design or require additional work in the client/server to account for it.  For example, using the [library.proto](https://github.com/googleapis/googleapis/blob/master/google/example/library/v1/library.proto) as an example, it organizes resources into a resource hierarchy `/shelves/{shelf_id}/books/{book_id}`.  That means creating a new shelf will create a new resource with `name = /shelves/{shelf_id}`.  If this name is later passed as the `parent` field in `ListBooksRequest` message, it won't work because the json transcoding won't recognize `/v1/{parent=shelves/*}/books` as a valid mapping.  The best I can do is `/v1/shelves/{parent}/books`.  This means I can either:
1. Try and add server side logic to automatically convert parent field value from "{shelf_id}" to "/shelves/{shelf_id}".
2. Require clients to perform the name/parent conversion logic to meet the requirements for the expected resource name rather than the server.
3. Don't maintain collection names in the path of the resource names.  For example, book names would be `/{shelf_id}/{book_id}` rather than `/shelves/{shelf_id}/books/{book_id}`.

All of these options seem pretty bad.

review_comments: I'm a bit confused by this, aren't these route values provided by the user? The user is going to use "book.name" not some internal encoded string like this.

Look at the code immediately below your comment. The RewriteVariableAction is called and reconstructs these internal values into a value set to `book.name`.

I've also made the comment at the top of JsonTranscodingRouteAdapter more detailed.

Figured it out by looking at the test logs, we are constructing the routing template for the routing middleware which is what looks at the route provided by the user and matches + constructs the `RouteValueDictionary`.
e.g. we generate `"/v1/{name.last_name}/complex_greeter/{**__Complex_name.first_name_3:regex(b/c/d/two$)}"` and pass that to routing for matching.
This is internal, so `List<T>` is preferred
I used `IList<T>` because there are places where it could be called with an array.

This runs for each route on startup and is then cached. Requests reuse the adapter.

It's not performance-critical.

Oh, and the adapted routes passed to ASP.NET Core still use DFA route matching. e.g. `/v1/{book=shelves/*/books/*}` turns into `/v1/shelves/{param1}/books/{param2}`. As fast as you can get. There is an extra string allocation to resolve the final route value, e.g. `$"shelves/{param1}/books/{param2}"`, but there is no way around that.

It doesn't do something inefficient like map a catch-all route and then reimplement matching in the gRPC JSON transcoding library.

Note that multi-segment route parameters are definitely the minority. Most APIs will use routes that look just like the ones in ASP.NET Core, e.g. `"/v1/shelves/{param1}/books/{param2}"`.
Is this a per message allocation? Can it be cached or avoided?
This is only called on startup.

```suggestion
    [InlineData("/a:foo}", "Path template wasn't parsed to the end.")]
    public void Error(string pattern, string errorMessage)
```

This is per request allocations, and should be reduced if possible.
The `object[]` is completely temporary, so a good candidate for using a pool.
The `catchAllSuffix` part could be able to be rewritten to not need the `Substring` since you know about it before creating the rewrite action.

> The object[] is completely temporary, so a good candidate for using a pool.

It's never going to be larger than 32 items. And usually much smaller than tat. Pooling would cost more time than it saves.

> The catchAllSuffix part could be able to be rewritten to not need the Substring since you know about it before creating the rewrite action.

It's required here because the suffix comes from the catch-all route value, not the template. It has to happen per request.
Oh I see, it comes from the route values, so technically you could substring the last route value instead of the final result which would result in smaller allocations
